paragraphs.text: Not by a call from God, but of his own mind, as some think, presuming upon his strength, and therefore justly deserted and foiled. Or if by some weighty occasion, as others hold, yet not purposely to see and have this harlot; for that had been to "make provision for the flesh, to fulfil the lusts thereof," {Rom 13:14} which scarce befalleth a godly man to do. But accidentally casting his eyes upon this Circe, he was enchanted by her, finding her fair face to be like a glass, wherein, while larks gaze, they are taken in a day-net.
paragraphs.anchor: Then went Samson to Gaza.

paragraphs.text: “ Quid facies faciem Veneris cum veneris ante!
Non sedeas, sed eas: non pereas per eas. ”
And went in unto her.] Carried away by human infirmity, forgetting God and his high calling, this Iudex et Senex falleth into the foul sin of fornication.
“ Laenam non potuit, potuit superare leaenam:
Quem fera non potuit vincere, vicit hera. ”
See their sedulity and Samson’s security, but especially God’s superabundant mercy: {1Ti 1:14} the riches of his grace cast in over and above desert or desire. {Eph 2:7 Rom 5:20}
paragraphs.anchor: And they compassed him in.

paragraphs.text: From the bed of fornication, where the Spirit had screeched out unto him, "Oh, do not this abominable thing!" {Jer 44:4} Nevertheless he did it; and yet by the instinct of the same Spirit, who might justly have loathed his lodging, he arose and prepared to be gone. God dealeth not with his people according to their sins, but beareth long with their evil manners.
paragraphs.anchor: And arose at midnight.

paragraphs.text: The watchmen sleeping the while, or not daring to stir. A figure of Christ’s glorious resurrection, maugre the malice of earth and of hell.
paragraphs.anchor: And took the doors of the gate of the city.

paragraphs.text: By an act of stupendous strength - never the like heard of he carrieth away the gates wherein they thought to have encaged him. If a temptation has drawn any of us aside to lie down to sin, it is happy for us if we can arise ere we be surprised by judgment.
paragraphs.anchor: Bar and all.

paragraphs.text: Or, Over against Hebron, though some miles distant; for Hebron was fourteen miles from Gaza, saith Adricomius.
paragraphs.anchor: Up to the top of a hill that is before Hebron.

paragraphs.text: Not long afterwards, but before he had soundly repented of his former faultiness; the orifice of his lust being not yet stopped. So Lot committed incest two nights together. But of Judah it is expressly noted that, coming to a sight of his sin with Tamar, he "knew her again no more." {Gen 38:26}
paragraphs.anchor: And it came to pass afterward.

paragraphs.text: A pleasant place, full of vines and myrtles. To Samson it proved a valley of vanity.
paragraphs.anchor: In the valley of Sorek.

paragraphs.text: A fit name for a harlot, for it comes from Dalal, which signifieth to exhaust, or to impoverish. It is the property of such female sinners to exhaust the purse, drain the strength, dry up the credit, waste the all of the mightiest Samsons. The Rabbis make Delilah to have been his wife, and further say, that he taught her the law of Moses before he took her; but none of this is likely to be true.
paragraphs.anchor: Whose name was Delilah.

paragraphs.text: Two engines they use against Samson, Muliere et Munere: these were as bad as those two great pieces of ordnance cast by Alphonsus, duke of Ferrara, the one whereof he called the Earthquake, and the other Grandiabolo, or the great devil.
paragraphs.anchor: Entice him, and see wherein, &c.

paragraphs.text: Or, To humble him. They would not say to kill him, lest that should sound harsh in her ears who had entertained him for her paramour, and pretended love to him, but only to tame him, and take him a link lower, as they say.
paragraphs.anchor: That we may bind him to afflict him.

paragraphs.text: Which is held to be more than a thousand pounds. Wicked men care not what they part with, nor how they lavish out of the bag, for the satisfying of their lusts. Haman offered ten thousand talents to have the Jews rooted out. Decius Mundus, a nobleman of Rome, offered Paulina six thousand pounds for one night’s lodging with her, as Josephus reporteth. {a}
paragraphs.anchor: Eleven hundred pieces of silver.

paragraphs.text: {a} Lib. xviii, cap. 4.

It is likely that Samson at some time or other had given out that his great strength lay in something whereof he might be deprived, though he never yet told wherein; and was now most hardly drawn to it.
paragraphs.anchor: Tell me, I pray thee, wherein thy great strength.

paragraphs.text: This he said for a put off, or as intending to make himself sport with her. But he should have remembered that God’s children will not lie. {Isa 63:8}
paragraphs.anchor: And Samson said unto her, If they bind me with seven green withs.

paragraphs.text: So heathen histories tell us of Hercules, that he was miserably enslaved and abused by his mistress, Omphale Queen of Lydia. Amantes amentes. How was Antony befooled by Cleopatra, {a} and the Persian kings by their concubines, being captivarum suarum captivi! they commanded the whole world, but were commanded by those minions.
paragraphs.anchor: And she bound him with them.

paragraphs.text: {a} Plutarch.
But durst not for their ears show themselves, till the experiment should prove true, and they be sure to overcome him.
paragraphs.anchor: Now there were men lying in wait.

paragraphs.text: Delilah may give Samson the lie: she may say anything, do anything to him: as Omphale or Jole might clap Hercules on the cheeks, or beat him about the head with her slipper: whereas, if another had done half so much, it would not have been borne with more patience than Robert Earl of Essex took a cuff on the ear from Queen Elizabeth. He laid his hand upon his sword, saith Mr Camden, and swore a great oath that he neither could nor would swallow so great an indignity, nor would he have borne it at King Henry VIII’s hand.
paragraphs.anchor: And told me lies.

paragraphs.text: See Jdg 16:7.
paragraphs.anchor: And he said unto her.

paragraphs.text: This he little thought of. No more do evil doers consider that the wrath of God and rage of all the creatures are ready prest to surprise them.
paragraphs.anchor: And there were liers in wait.

paragraphs.text: See Jdg 16:10.
paragraphs.anchor: And told me lies.

paragraphs.text: Here he came nearer the business than before; till at length she had his whole heart out. Well might Terence call harlots Cruces.
paragraphs.anchor: The seven locks of my head.

paragraphs.text: And he awaked out of his sleep.] The Philistines durst not meddle with him though asleep: no more than men dare venture upon a sleeping lion.

This was, it seems, a great word in Samson’s mouth, "I love thee dearly, Delilah." This she twitteth him with, as if only from the teeth outward: and that he did not Medullitus et animitus eam amare. In amore sese comitantur ερως ετ ερις.
paragraphs.anchor: How canst thou say, I love thee?

paragraphs.text: Coarctaret, pene cogeret. She gave him no rest or respite, Ut anima eius tantum non enecaretur, so that he was even weary of his life through her importunity, to the which at length he yielded: as afterwards Alexander the Great burned the fair city Persepolis, at the motion of a strumpet, upon whom he impotently doated.
paragraphs.anchor: When she pressed him daily with her words.

paragraphs.text: Of Tamerlane, that warlike Scythian, it is storied, that he nourished his hair, which his mother coming of the race of Samson, as he gave it out, willed him to do in token of his descent. This was the cause that made him to be more respected of his men of war, most part of them believing that in those hairs was some rare virtue, or rather some fatal destiny. {a}
paragraphs.anchor: There hath not come a razor upon my head, &c.

paragraphs.text: {a} Turk. Hist., 236.

Whoredom indeed had "taken away his heart," {Hos 4:11} had infatuated and besotted him, as it is the nature of these sensual sins to do; these "lusts of the flesh that war against the soul." {1Pe 2:12}
paragraphs.anchor: And when Delilah saw that he had told her all his heart.

paragraphs.text: Money they knew to be the monarch of this world, and to bear the mastery; but especially with such Poscinummiae, et Crumenimulgae as Delilah was.
paragraphs.anchor: And brought money in their hand.

paragraphs.text: He sleepeth, but his enemies are waking and working against him: so are the antichristian rout against the Church of Christ. Oh pray, pray, said an eminent Dutch divine, Pontifex enim Rom. et Concilium Tridentinum mira molluntur.
paragraphs.anchor: And she made him sleep upon her knees.

paragraphs.text: And here Samson, simul comam atque coronam amisit, saith Jerome; he lost his hair and his crown, that is, his stupendous strength, together. And with this history of Samson agreeth that which Ovid {a} writeth of Nisus, king of the Megarensians, with his purple hair stolen from him by his own daughter, to his utter undoing. The devil loveth to be God’s ape. Quid enim Satanas impie non imitetur? saith Junius here.
paragraphs.anchor: To shave off the seven locks of his head.

paragraphs.text: Trudere et trudendo excitare, ut sibi caveret fuga; to bind him, and then to rouse him by jogging and thrusting him.
paragraphs.anchor: And she began to afflict him.

paragraphs.text: {a} Metam. 8.

After which, all miseries came rushing in upon him, as by a sluice: according to that of the prophet, "Woe be unto you when I depart from you": του λογου ησυχαζοντος. When the Godhead withdrew but a while from our Saviour in the garden, and upon the cross, then began his sorrows and sufferings.
paragraphs.anchor: That the Lord was departed from him.

paragraphs.text: These eyes of his were the first offenders that betrayed him to lust; {Jdg 16:1} and now they are first pulled out, and he led a blind captive to Gaza, where he was first captivated to his lust. The loss of his eyes showeth him his sin, saith one. {a} Neither could he see how ill he had done, till he saw not. Muleasses king of Tunis, expelled his kingdom for whoredom, had his eyes put out with a burning hot iron, but was not brought thereby to a sight of his sin.
paragraphs.anchor: Took him, and put out his eyes.

paragraphs.text: Who had suffered himself to be bound with the green withs of sensual delights.
paragraphs.anchor: And bound him with fetters of brass.

paragraphs.text: Like a slave, or rather like a horse: that he might earn his bread before he ate it. Yet by it, saith an interpreter, they chuckered themselves to think what use they should make herein of his great strength.
paragraphs.anchor: And he did grind in the prison house.

paragraphs.text: {a} Bp. Hall.

By this time Samson was thoroughly humbled, and "accepting the chastisement of his iniquity," found God favourable, whose property it is to comfort the abject, {2Co 7:6} and to do his people good when they are called outcasts; when men say, "This is Zion, whom no man seeketh after." {Jer 30:17} Samson repenting, reassumed his Nazariteship, and God was soon reconciled.
paragraphs.anchor: Howbeit the hair of his head began to grow again.

paragraphs.text: That is, To Triton, the idol af those maritime nations, which was a fish downward, whence also he had his name Dagon. See 1Sa 5:4. Diodorus Siculus calleth this idol Derceta; others, Leucothea.
paragraphs.anchor: For to offer a great sacrifice unto Dagon their god.

paragraphs.text: Ad celebranda hilaria. So the wild Irish when they go to rob, which they account no shame, pray to God that they may meet with a booty; and when they meet with it, they account it God’s gift, and rejoice exceedingly. {a}
paragraphs.anchor: And to rejoice.

paragraphs.text: {a} Camd., Britan. Irel., p. 144.
Magnates, magnetes; the multitude do as their rulers; and, as in beasts, the body followeth the head, so here.
paragraphs.anchor: And when the people saw him, they praised their god.

paragraphs.text: At feasts they had their γελωτοποιοι, such as made them merry. The Emperors of Rome presented the people with strange sights, as of lions, bears, panthers, tigers, &c., to exhilarate them: they also led their enemies before them in triumph: which Cleopatra not able to endure, killed herself: So did not Samson, but became the subject of his enemies’ scorn and malice, as did likewise Christ. {Mat 27:29-31}
paragraphs.anchor: Call for Samson, that he may make us sport.

paragraphs.text: Where he might best be seen: but God had a holy hand in it, for a further mischief unto them.
paragraphs.anchor: And they set him between the pillars.

paragraphs.text: And so rest me, who am wearied out, either with grinding in the prison, or now making sport.
paragraphs.anchor: That I may lean upon them.

paragraphs.text: Dagon’s temple: that where they had sinned, there they might suffer. So Ahab’s blood was licked up by dogs in the place where he had slain Naboth. {1Ki 21:19} So Henry III of France was stabbed to death in that very chamber where he had contrived the massacre of Paris.
paragraphs.anchor: Now the house.

paragraphs.text: Assembled they were, by an overruling Providence, that they might be "broken in pieces." {Isa 8:9} So were the Baalites in mount Carmel, {1Ki 18:40} and afterwards in the house of their god, to be slain by Jehu. And so were the refractory Jews besieged and taken by the Romans at the feast of the Passover, when they were met together out of all parts of the land.
paragraphs.anchor: Was full of men and women.

paragraphs.text: This was a prayer of faith, and a fruit of his repentance. Nunquam sero, si serio.
paragraphs.anchor: And Samson called unto the Lord.

paragraphs.text: Orat et laborat: the heathens could say, Admota manu invocanda est Minerva. Men must pray, but with it do their endeavour; for God is not mocked. They that will be wise to salvation, must not only beg, but dig. {Pro 2:3-5} Samson first prayed, and then bowed himself with all his might. {Jdg 16:30}
paragraphs.anchor: And Samson took hold.

paragraphs.text: Heb., Let my soul die {as Num 23:10} with the Philistines, - yet not as the Philistines, but the death of the righteous, who hath hope in his death, - to {Pro 14:32} destroy these Philistines, God’s enemies, out of a zeal of God’s glory.
paragraphs.anchor: Let me die with the Philistines.

paragraphs.text: He devoted himself to death, not out of despair, or for vainglory, as some heathens did - Codrus the king of Athens, Decius the Roman Consul, &c. - but by an extraordinary instinct of God’s Spirit, and for a public good: as that Christian soldier did, who at the siege of Buda, to prevent the taking of the town, threw himself down from the wall, together with the dog, as he called him, - the Turk who had first got to the top of it, and set up the Turkish colours there; whereby the town was saved. Samson knew that he should die with the Philistines, Simili quidem poena, sed dissimili culpa, et diverso fine ac fato. Multum interest et qualia quis, et quisque patiatur, saith Augustine.
These all died alike, but not for a like cause, or with like comfort.

Lords and the common people perished together. So they did at Fidenae in the days of Tiberius, where the amphitheatre fell at a sight of sword playing, and destroyed thirty thousand people, {a} So at the fall of Blackfriars, many Papists were slain at a Mass: Drury the priest had his sermon and his brains knocked out of his head together. Let those that sport themselves with oaths as the Philistines did with Samson, beware; it will pull the house about their ears. {Zec 5:4}
paragraphs.anchor: And the house fell upon the lords, &c.

paragraphs.text: A type of Christ herein. {Heb 2:14} Death also is to a saint the accomplishment of mortification. {Rom 6:7}
paragraphs.anchor: So the dead.

paragraphs.text: {a} Sueton.
An example of brotherly kindness.
paragraphs.anchor: Then his brethren.
